sections.title: Introduction to the Prohibitions of Avoda Zara
sections.html:
In order for Israel to be able to cleave to the One God and draw blessing to themselves and to the whole world, they must distance themselves from any trace of avoda zara (idolatry). Thereby they will be able to absorb the light of God, walk in the ways of God by doing righteousness and justice, understand His Torah and fulfil His mitzvot, settle the land and be fruitful and multiply in it. And blessing will increase in agriculture, in industry, in science, in society and in art, until we merit the coming of our righteous Mashiaḥ, and all the inhabitants of the world will want to walk in the ways of God.

Therefore, in addition to the prohibition of worshipping avoda zara itself, God commanded Israel several prohibitions:

1) To destroy the idols, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire" (above 3:9).

2) Not to derive benefit from avoda zara and from its accessories, its ornaments and its offerings, as will be explained further on in this chapter.

3) Not to vow or swear in the name of avoda zara, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And make no mention of the name of other gods; it shall not be heard from your mouth." This includes not causing gentiles to swear by their idols (below 11:3).

4) In addition to the mitzva to destroy the idols themselves, there is a mitzva to treat them with contempt in order to destroy their name, as it is stated (Devarim 12:3): "And you shall destroy their name from that place." Destroying the name is also accomplished by changing their name to a derogatory one, as it is stated (ibid. 7:26): "You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a ḥerem (a banned thing)" (below 14:1).

5) Not to take an interest in avoda zara, lest one be enticed after it, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols" (below chapter 13).

6) Not to benefit avoda zara, that is, not to donate to it, and not even to buy something from which a tax is paid for its upkeep (below 11:6).

7) It is also forbidden to bring a gentile's statue into one's house, as it is stated (Devarim 7:26): "And you shall not bring an abomination into your house." The Sages added a prohibition against renting a dwelling to an idol worshipper who customarily brings an idolatrous statue into his house (below 11:9).

8) Even for decoration, the Torah forbade making statues in the image of the attendants in the upper realm, such as angels, and in the lower realm, such as the sun and moon, and in the image of a human being, so that people should not err after them, as it is stated (Shemot 20:19): "You shall not make [gods] with Me" (below 15:1-7).

9) The Sages added a prohibition against Jews doing things that look like avoda zara, because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers) (below 12:2-3).

In this chapter we will deal with the prohibition of deriving benefit from avoda zara, and in the following chapters the laws of the other safeguards will be explained.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Deriving Benefit
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to destroy the statues of idols, and it is forbidden to derive benefit from them; one who transgresses and benefits from them is liable to lashes. Even if the statue was made of silver or gold, it is forbidden to melt it down and benefit from its silver or gold, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25-26): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold on them and take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. And you shall not bring an abomination into your house and become a ḥerem like it; you shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a ḥerem." And it is likewise stated (Devarim 13:18): "And nothing of the ḥerem shall cleave to your hand."

The prohibition of benefit includes four categories: 1) the statues of their gods; 2) their accessories, the implements of their worship; 3) their ornaments, their decorations; 4) offerings, the sacrifices offered to them:

1) The statues of their gods are the statues and objects in which, idol worshippers believe, the power of the gods resides, and which have the power to benefit their worshippers. These include statues in the form of a human being or an animal, asherah trees, and all other things in which idol worshippers believe. For example, if an idol worshipper set up a brick and said to it, "You are my god," or bowed down to it, the brick became an idol and is forbidden for benefit.

2) Their accessories are the implements of their worship, that is, the implements with which idol worship is performed, such as censers for burning incense and a knife for slaughtering sacrifices.

3) The ornaments of the idols are the garments with which the statues are clothed, the crown placed on their head, and anything similar. But the garments of the priests who serve them are not considered ornaments of the idols, and are permitted for benefit (Tosafot; Rosh, Avoda Zara 4:1).

4) Offerings, that is, sacrifices offered to the idols, such as animals slaughtered in their honour or foods offered to them (as explained in note 3).

Since it is forbidden to derive benefit from these four categories even after they have been destroyed, they must be destroyed in a manner that makes it impossible to benefit from the material of which they are made. Therefore, if they were made of wood or of other materials that burn, one burns them and scatters their ashes so as not to benefit from them. Even while disposing of them, one must take care not to benefit from the fire in which they are burned. If one baked bread or cooked a dish over a fire of the wood of avoda zara, they are forbidden for benefit (SA YD 142:1, 4). If they were made of metal that does not burn, such as silver and gold, one must grind them and scatter their particles to the wind, or throw them into the sea in a place from which people will not be able to retrieve them, in which case there is no need to grind them (SA YD 146:14; Shakh 13).1

sections.title: Idols of Wood and Stone That Become Forbidden for Benefit
sections.html:
Statues of gentiles become forbidden for benefit from the time the work of making them is completed. But a statue that a Jew made becomes forbidden only from the time he begins to worship it, since Jews in general are repelled by avoda zara, and as long as he has not worshipped the statue there is still a chance that he will repent and not worship it. The accessories and ornaments of avoda zara, even those of gentiles, do not become forbidden until they have been used in worship (Avoda Zara 51b; SA YD 139:1).

Anything in which there is no handiwork of man, that is, which was not made by man but is so by the nature of its creation, is permitted for benefit even though it was worshipped. Therefore, mountains, hills, rivers and springs that were worshipped are permitted for benefit; and likewise mountain stones that broke off by themselves, remained in their place and were worshipped are permitted. If one overlaid a mountain with gold and it was worshipped, only the overlay is forbidden for benefit. Similarly, if one placed a statue on a stone or drew on a stone for the sake of avoda zara, the stone is forbidden as long as the statue or drawing is on it, and after it is removed the stone is permitted. If an idol worshipper built a house for avoda zara, the house becomes forbidden for benefit. If he built an ordinary house and brought a statue into it, as long as the statue is inside, the house is forbidden for benefit; once it is removed, the house is permitted for benefit. If he built an ordinary house and plastered or whitewashed it for the sake of avoda zara, one removes the plaster or the whitewash and the house is permitted (SA YD 145:1-5).

If one planted a tree in order to worship it, the tree is forbidden for benefit, for it is considered something in which there is human handiwork; and this is the asherah, which there is a mitzva to destroy and uproot so that it does not grow again (Avoda Zara 45b; SA YD 146:15). But if one planted an ordinary tree, it is considered something in which there is no human handiwork, and if he afterwards began to worship it, all that grew on it before that is permitted for benefit, and what grows on it from the time he began to worship it is forbidden for benefit. If one bowed down to an animal, it does not become forbidden. If one slaughtered an animal for the sake of avoda zara, it becomes forbidden for benefit, and this is an offering of avoda zara (SA YD 145:6-8).

Included in the prohibition of benefiting from idols is that it is forbidden to sit in the shade of an asherah tree, that is, in the shade of a tree that is worshipped or under which an idol has been placed. Even when the shade of the asherah extends into the public domain it is forbidden to sit under it; and if a public road passes under the shade of the asherah, if there is another road there as short and convenient, one should take the other road. And if there is no other road there as short and convenient, one may go on his way under the shade of the asherah, and he should run there, to show that he has no interest in benefiting from the shade of the asherah (Avoda Zara 48a-b; SA YD 142:9). Even a tree that is not an asherah, but was planted beside the idol to serve as an ornament for the avoda zara, is forbidden for benefit, and it is forbidden to sit in its shade, by the law of the ornaments of avoda zara (SA YD 142:13).

Trees planted in a garden adjacent to a house of avoda zara, since they were not intended to be an ornament for the avoda zara itself, may be benefited from, as may their shade (Ritva). However, when those present there appear to want to draw near to the avoda zara, it is forbidden because of mar'it ayin (below 12:3).2

sections.title: Offerings to Avoda Zara
sections.html:
Sacrifices and offerings (takrovot) that were offered to avoda zara are forbidden for benefit forever. And although an idol worshipper can nullify his statues, as well as the statue's accessories and its ornaments, whereby they become permitted for benefit, he cannot nullify the offerings, and they remain forbidden forever (below section 5).

The sacrifices become forbidden for benefit on condition that they were "ke-ein penim" (like the inner service), that is, that a cultic act was performed with them similar to the services that were performed in the Temple. Therefore, idol worshippers who were accustomed, whenever they slaughtered animals for food, to intend that the slaughter be for the sake of the idols—all their meat is forbidden for benefit by the law of an offering, for slaughter is a service "ke-ein penim".3

Those who bring offerings and place them before the idols: if they are like the things that were brought in the Temple, that is, animal meat, fine flours, oils and fruits of the seven species, then even without an additional cultic act, bringing them is considered "ke-ein penim" and they become forbidden for benefit (SA YD 139:3). But other fruits, flowers and candles brought as an offering do not become forbidden for benefit (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh and SA YD 139:3; the Rambam is stringent).4

sections.title: Nullification of a Gentile's Avoda Zara
sections.html:
A gentile's avoda zara can be nullified by a gentile, and thereby it becomes permitted for benefit, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold on them and take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it." As long as the statues are "their gods", it is forbidden to take them and benefit from them; but if they nullified them, since they are no longer their gods, there is no prohibition of benefit in them (Avoda Zara 52b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 8:8).

The nullification is accomplished by an act of an idol-worshipping gentile that damages the statue and thereby expresses decisively that he does not believe in it, for example if he cut off the tip of its ear, or its nose or its finger. Likewise, if he struck it in its face until its form changed, even though he did not remove anything from it, he has nullified it. But if, out of anger at the idol, he spat on the statue, relieved himself on it or dragged it on the floor, it is not nullified, for idol worshippers sometimes did this in their anger, and afterwards were reconciled and returned to worshipping it. Therefore, only an act of actual damage to the body of the statue expresses a decision to nullify it, and removes from it the prohibition of benefit.

Even when the gentile nullified the statue against his will, his nullification is valid, since he understood that he was performing an act that nullifies its status as an idol. However, only a gentile "who knows the nature of avoda zara", that is, one who worships avoda zara, can nullify it. And even if he worships a different idol, since in general he is an idol worshipper, he can nullify them. But a gentile who does not worship idols cannot nullify them. A gentile minor or a mentally incompetent person cannot nullify avoda zara, since he does not understand the meaning of his actions (Avoda Zara 43a; 52b; Rambam 8:9; SA YD 146:5).

If the gentile nullified the statue, its accessories and ornaments are also permitted. However, the offerings that were offered before it remain forbidden forever. If the gentile nullified the idol's implements of worship, only the implements he nullified are permitted, but the statue and its other accessories and ornaments remain forbidden (Avoda Zara 52b; SA YD 139:2; 146:13).

Statues that broke by themselves are forbidden for benefit, since they were not nullified. Likewise, statues and altars whose owners fled because of war are forbidden for benefit. But if their owners could have returned to worship them after the war and did not return to worship them, and likewise statues and implements of worship that were abandoned because over the generations people stopped believing in them, they are nullified and it is permitted to benefit from them (Avoda Zara 53b; SA YD 146:10-11).5 Accordingly, it seems that ancient temples and statues that people stopped worshipping, even though it is not known that they intended to abandon them, are permitted for benefit; for since much time has passed since they were worshipped, the heirs of their worshippers have abandoned them completely and the prohibition has lapsed (see below 12:8 regarding entering these places).

If the gentile sold the statue, whether to a gentile or to a Jew, it is not nullified, for the one who sells it hopes that a buyer will be found for the statue who will worship it (Avoda Zara 53a; SA YD 146:8). If the gentile sold the statue without specification, the money he received for it is forbidden for benefit, for perhaps he intended to use the money for the needs of avoda zara. But if the gentile sold the statue or its accessories in order to use the money for secular purposes, the money he received is permitted (Avoda Zara 64a; SA YD 144:1).6

sections.title: A Jew's Avoda Zara Can Never Be Nullified
sections.html:
A Jew's avoda zara can never be nullified, for from the moment the Jew began to worship it there is a Torah obligation to destroy it, and consequently it is forbidden for benefit forever. And what we learned, that a gentile's avoda zara can be nullified, is because there is no obligation upon the gentile to destroy the avoda zara; consequently, if he nullifies it, it is nullified, and thereby its material becomes permitted (SA YD 146:1). The accessories and ornaments of a Jew's avoda zara likewise are not nullified, for there is an obligation to destroy them, and consequently there is no possibility of nullifying them and thereby permitting them (Gra 146:2). Even a Jewish apostate who is devoted to avoda zara cannot nullify avoda zara (Taz 139:1).

If a Jew sold avoda zara or its accessories, the money he received in exchange for them is also forbidden for benefit; and likewise if he exchanged them for something else, such as an animal, the animal also becomes forbidden for benefit, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25-26): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire… And you shall not bring an abomination into your house and become a ḥerem like it": whatever you receive for it will be forbidden for benefit like it (Avoda Zara 54b; SA YD 144:1; 145:9).

The Sages decreed that even a gentile's avoda zara that came into the possession of a Jew, since it became his, he is obligated to destroy it, and there is no possibility of its being nullified by a gentile; lest, if people are lenient with it, they come to be lenient also with a Jew's avoda zara, which cannot be nullified (Semag; SA YD 146:1-2).7

sections.title: The Prohibition of Mixtures of Avoda Zara
sections.html:
Because of the severity of the prohibition of avoda zara, the Sages ordained that avoda zara is not nullified even in a thousand: if an idolatrous statue became mixed with similar statues made for decoration and not for worship, all are forbidden for benefit. If a spoon that was used for idolatrous worship became mixed with ordinary spoons, all are forbidden for benefit. And likewise if a piece of meat that was offered to avoda zara became mixed with a thousand pieces, all are forbidden for benefit (Avoda Zara 74a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:9; SA YD 140:1).

As we have learned (in section 2), it is forbidden to benefit from things of avoda zara; but when it is not a matter of an actual mixture of avoda zara, but only of something that was caused by avoda zara, the rule is "zeh ve-zeh gorem, mutar" (where this and that cause it, it is permitted). That is to say, when two factors contributed to the creation of something, one forbidden and one permitted, the resulting product is permitted. Therefore, although it is forbidden to feed an animal vegetables that were offered as an offering to avoda zara, and it is forbidden to fertilise a field with an offering to avoda zara, if an animal was fed an offering, it is permitted to eat its meat or drink its milk, because they were created through a combination of permitted and forbidden foods. And if a field was fertilised with an offering to avoda zara, it is permitted to sow in the field, since the field was enriched by permitted fertilisers that accumulated in it naturally and also by fertiliser of avoda zara (Avoda Zara 49a; SA YD 142:11; see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 34:6; Pesaḥ 8:5, note 6).

sections.title: Benefit from the Music, Scent and Sight of Avoda Zara
sections.html:
It is forbidden to enjoy hearing songs and melodies that are sung or played for avoda zara, and likewise it is forbidden to enjoy seeing the images of avoda zara or smelling the incense burned to it (Rabbenu Yeruḥam 17:5; SA YD 108:7; 142:15). And one who turns himself to enjoy them or gaze at them transgresses a Torah prohibition, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols" (Shabbat 149a; below 13:1).

One who needs to pass on his way near a place of worship at a time when the scent of incense being burned there rises from it, or when the sound of singing or music being sung or played before the avoda zara is heard from it, or in a place where he sees its ornaments, may pass on condition that he does not intend to benefit from it, and also that it is not inevitable that he will benefit from it; for example, if a desire to enjoy it arises in him, he can block his nose so as not to smell, or stop his ears so as not to hear, or turn his gaze so as not to see. In that case, as long as he does not intend to benefit, even if he smells, hears or sees, he is permitted to pass. But if he cannot avoid smelling, hearing or seeing, then even if he does not intend to benefit, he is forbidden to pass there. All the more so it is forbidden for him to pass there when he intends to benefit (Rabbenu Yeruḥam ibid.; Shakh 142:34). The law of enjoying music and pictures that were recorded or photographed in a place of worship will be explained below (13:8).8

sections.title: Performing Mitzvot with Things of Avoda Zara
sections.html:
All things that did not become forbidden for benefit even though they were worshipped, such as things in which there is no human handiwork, like stones and animals (above section 3), or that were nullified by gentiles (above section 5), since they were worshipped, became repulsive and disqualified for the Temple service (Arukh Ha-shulḥan He-atid, Hilkhot Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 55:20). Therefore, if one bowed down to his animal, it is disqualified as a sacrifice, and priestly garments are not made from its wool. If one bowed down to mountain stones, they are disqualified for building the altar. If one bowed down to a spring that flows in his courtyard, all the water that was in it at that time is disqualified for the water libation. And likewise an asherah tree that gentiles worshipped and afterwards nullified—logs of wood are not brought from it for the altar (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 4:7).

The Rishonim disagreed whether these things are also forbidden for other mitzvot, such as for a shofar, a lulav and tzitzit. In practice it is ruled that even if they belonged to a gentile and he nullified them, so that they are permitted for benefit, they have become repulsive for a mitzva, and le-khatḥila (ab initio) one should not use them for the needs of a mitzva.

Be-di'avad (after the fact), if one used them for a mitzva, the law depends on whether they can be nullified or not. If they belong to a Jew, he has not fulfilled the mitzva, for since there is an obligation to destroy them from the world, they are considered as if destroyed, and consequently it is impossible to fulfil a mitzva with them. But if they belong to a gentile, since they can be nullified they are not considered as if destroyed; and even though in practice they were not nullified and are therefore forbidden for benefit, be-di'avad he has fulfilled his obligation of performing the mitzva with them, because performing mitzvot is not considered benefit.9

sections.title: Converting a Church into a Synagogue
sections.html:
The poskim disagreed whether it is permitted to convert a church that has been nullified into a synagogue. Some forbid it, because after the building was used for the needs of avoda zara, it became repulsive for the needs of a mitzva. Indeed, by being sold for any use, it is no longer considered an accessory of avoda zara, and it is permitted to benefit from it; but just as it is forbidden to light in a synagogue candles that were used for avoda zara, even if they were nullified from serving it (SA OḤ 154:11), so it is forbidden to make a synagogue out of a building that served as a church and was nullified (Eliyahu Rabba 154:15).

Some say that it is permitted to convert a church into a synagogue, for only movable things that were used for avoda zara become repulsive for a mitzva, but a building attached to the ground does not become repulsive. In addition, it was not the building itself that was worshipped, and therefore from the time it ceased to serve avoda zara, it is permitted to convert it into a synagogue (Magen Avraham 154:17).

In practice, le-khatḥila one should be stringent not to make a synagogue out of a building that served as a church, and be-di'avad, if it was done, one may pray in it.10

sections.title: Candles and Decorations Manufactured for Avoda Zara
sections.html:
If one designates an animal to be sacrificed to avoda zara, then from the time a preparatory act is performed with it, for example if the priests shore its wool in honour of the idol, even if the owner of the animal changes his mind and no longer wishes to sacrifice it to avoda zara, it is forbidden to be offered on the altar to God.

However, all this applies specifically to offering on the altar, because it is repulsive to offer before God in the Temple an animal that was designated to be sacrificed to avoda zara. But it is permitted to use candles that were designated to be lit before the idol for lighting Shabbat or Ḥanuka candles. Similarly, it is permitted to decorate the sukka with decorations that were manufactured for decorating avoda zara and churches.11

sections.title: Wigs Whose Hair Comes from India
sections.html:
In 5764 (2004), a controversy arose concerning wigs whose hair is brought from India. It became clear that some of the hair is brought from the area of the city of Tirupati in southern India, where there is a place of worship visited by tens of millions of people a year, many of whom shave the hair of their heads in preparation for coming before the idol. The hair belonging to the place of worship is afterwards sold to the global wig industry. Those who forbade argued that shaving the hair is a cultic act, and is consequently considered like slaughter, whereby the hair becomes forbidden for benefit. And although the Rishonim disagreed whether in such a case the hair becomes forbidden, those who forbade ruled according to the stringent view. On the other hand, those who permitted inquired of people familiar with their religion, and it became clear that the shaving is not a cultic act but only a preparation for coming before the idol in submission, and consequently, according to all opinions, the hair does not become forbidden for benefit.

In practice, even if we take into account the view of the stringent authorities, since there are two doubts in this law, even when it is known that the wig's hair was brought from Tirupati, the wig is permitted. All the more so when the source of the hair is not known, for then there are three doubts, as explained in the note.12
